summary: Deep technical discussion focused on private VPC networking for Redwood Private deployment at Aurelius Financial. Covered PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway options, NAT and egress patterns, subnet sizing, DNS resolution strategies (split-horizon, conditional forwarding), cross-account VPC endpoints, and implications for runtime performance (KV cache locality, batching, quantization tradeoffs). Agreed next steps for benchmark runs, sharing CIDR info, and security artifacts.
topics: Runtime implications: KV cache, batching, latency
transcript:
00:00 Maya Chen: Hi everyone, thanks for joining. We have about an hour to go over private VPC networking and how it ties into the runtime behavior. Quick intros?
00:08 Sasha Ivanov: Sasha here, CTO at Aurelius. We run a mixture of prod workloads in AWS and a few on-prem pockets.
00:14 Priya Patel: Priya, infra lead. I'll own the VPC config and networking.
00:17 Liam O'Connor: Liam, security. I'll focus on KMS, audit logs, and egress policies.
00:22 Diego Alvarez: Diego from Redwood SE, I'll walk through networking options and how they impact latency and KV cache.
00:28 Maya Chen: Great. High level: Aurelius wants Redwood Private in their AWS account with no internet-facing interfaces; we're here to align on PrivateLink, NAT, subnets, DNS, and perf tradeoffs.
00:40 Priya Patel: Correct. Also need to understand cross-account endpoints — we'll likely want Redwood control plane in our account for auditability.
00:48 Diego Alvarez: We support both models: customer-managed control plane (in your account) or a customer VPC with PrivateLink endpoints back to Redwood-managed control plane. For strict isolation the former is cleaner but heavier to operate.
01:05 Sasha Ivanov: Can you explain the PrivateLink vs Transit Gateway tradeoff? Which one gives lower latency for inference traffic?
01:12 Diego Alvarez: Sure. PrivateLink creates ENIs and VPC endpoints in your subnets — that keeps traffic within the AWS fabric and is usually lower latency because it's peer-to-peer to our service endpoints. Transit Gateway is better for hub-and-spoke if you have many VPCs and need centralized routing, but adds an extra hop which can increase p99s slightly depending on TGW attachments. For inference where p50/p90 matters, PrivateLink often gives more predictable latency.
01:37 Priya Patel: If we go PrivateLink, do we need NAT? We have strict egress rules.
01:42 Diego Alvarez: PrivateLink handles inbound to the service endpoint, but for things like model updates or container image pulls the worker nodes need egress. Options: use NAT Gateway with restrictive route tables, or use VPC endpoints for S3/ECR so you can keep everything private and avoid NAT entirely. For autoscaler control-plane callbacks we can also use interface endpoints.
02:05 Liam O'Connor: Our security team wants no internet egress from the subnets that host inference. We prefer VPC endpoints for S3/ECR and PrivateLink for Redwood. How does that affect cold-start latency and KV cache warmup?
02:18 Diego Alvarez: If you avoid NAT and use VPC endpoints for S3/ECR and PrivateLink for the API plane, you can still get good cold-start behavior. However, KV cache locality matters: if worker nodes are in private subnets without cross-AZ penalties and we pin them to the same AZs as Redis/kv-store (if you're using a managed KV), warmups are faster. If KV is across accounts or goes over TGW you could see an extra ~5-15ms per lookup depending on distance and concurrency.
02:48 Sasha Ivanov: Let's talk scale — we expect peak inference throughput of ~600 qps with 4k context. What sizing recommendations?
02:56 Diego Alvarez: For 600 qps at 4k, with our batching profile we'd recommend starting with dedicated pools of GPU instances; exact instance type depends on model and quantization. If you quantize 4-bit or use an 8-bit variant you can get 30-40% more throughput per GPU. Also configure autoscaling thresholds based on token-in-flight rather than just request count.
03:20 Priya Patel: On quantization: any runtime-level caveats when running in a customer VPC?
03:26 Diego Alvarez: No network-specific caveats. The main differences are model variant compatibility and that some kernels run faster on certain GPU types. Quantization changes memory footprint so your node sizing (EBS or instance memory) matters. If you use pinned memory with NVMe-backed instances we recommend larger ephemeral storage for swap-like workloads.
03:45 Maya Chen: Back to DNS — Priya, does Aurelius use private hosted zones or conditional forwarding to on-prem?
03:51 Priya Patel: We use split-horizon private hosted zones for our internal domains, and conditional forwarders to our on-prem DNS for some legacy names. We need Redwood to resolve internal service names for metrics collection and health checks.
04:03 Diego Alvarez: We can support private hosted zone delegation: create a private hosted zone in your account and associate the service VPCs. For cross-account we can use delegated zones or create resolver rules (Route 53 Resolver) with inbound endpoints. That approach works but you need to open the resolver endpoints and ensure security groups allow queries from the Redwood ENIs.
04:26 Liam O'Connor: Are there risks with split-horizon? We don't want inference nodes resolving public variants incorrectly.
04:31 Diego Alvarez: Right — that's why we recommend explicit VPC-level resolver rules. Keep the private zone authoritative for internal names and ensure forwarding rules for specific domains to the on-prem resolver. Also audit logs for Route 53 queries are helpful — we can collect and ship logs to your S3 bucket via VPC Flow Logs and resolver query logs.
04:56 Maya Chen: Let's touch on route tables and subnet design. Priya, how many AZs do you want to span?
05:02 Priya Patel: At least three for HA.
05:05 Diego Alvarez: Good. Put workers in private subnets in each AZ with route tables that point to NAT or endpoints as required. Interface endpoints for PrivateLink must be provisioned in the subnets where you want traffic to appear. For security we recommend separate subnets for system/control plane and runtime workers so you can apply stricter NACLs.
05:25 Sasha Ivanov: For cross-account PrivateLink — do we need AWS Resource Access Manager (RAM)?
05:30 Diego Alvarez: For interface endpoints it's done by creating an endpoint service in the provider account and giving permission for consumer accounts. RAM is more for sharing subnets or other resources; endpoint service permissions are sufficient. We'll share a step-by-step runbook.
05:45 Priya Patel: What about IP exhaustion with ENIs and endpoints? We have limited CIDR space.
05:50 Diego Alvarez: Each ENI uses IPs from the subnet; scale ENI consumption by using larger subnets or reserving IP pools. If CIDR is tight, consider using fewer, larger instance types per AZ or use proxying patterns to multiplex connections. We'll include a table showing expected ENI / IP consumption per worker fleet size.
06:08 Sasha Ivanov: Storage for logs and model artifacts — recommend private S3 access via VPC endpoint?
06:13 Diego Alvarez: Yes. Use VPC gateway endpoints for S3 and VPC interface endpoints for ECR, Secrets Manager, Systems Manager. That keeps everything inside AWS backbone and compatible with no-internet policies.
06:26 Liam O'Connor: How do you handle mutual auth for PrivateLink? We want mTLS and mutual TLS to the control plane.
06:33 Diego Alvarez: We support TLS and mTLS for control plane traffic. For PrivateLink you can terminate TLS at the endpoint service and have backend validation. We can also accept client certs tied to your SAML/IdP if you want mutual TLS plus IAM auth. We'll document the cert rotation steps.
06:53 Maya Chen: Switching gears — how does networking affect runtime token latency and KV cache?
06:58 Diego Alvarez: Two main things: KV cache locality and request path hops. If KV cache is colocated in the same AZ and you have low intra-AZ latency, cache hits are sub-ms or a few ms. If cache goes across TGW or to a different account, each lookup can add tens of ms. Since our serving runtime often does many KV lookups per token for attention caching (KV cache), those tens of ms add up to higher p99. Also, PrivateLink adds minimal extra latency but if you queue through a proxy that adds TLS decrypt/re-encrypt you'll see overhead.
07:30 Priya Patel: Is there a recommended cache architecture? Managed Redis in same VPC vs Redwood-owned cache?
07:36 Diego Alvarez: Both work. Customer-managed Redis in same account/AZ gives fastest path and simplifies compliance. Redwood can also offer an in-process KV cache or a co-located cache managed by us but that requires cross-account networking — slightly higher latency. For strict compliance and latency, customer-managed is preferred.
07:55 Sasha Ivanov: On batching — if we batch to improve throughput, that increases latency for single operations. How do you tune that in Private?
08:03 Diego Alvarez: We tune batching based on SLOs. Use adaptive batching: increase max batch size during high throughput to improve GPU utilization while keeping a hard latency ceiling. In practice you set target p95/p99 SLOs and we configure the serving runtime to prefer smaller batches below a latency threshold, and expand as queues build. Egress and KV lookups factor into that since they affect service time distributions.
08:28 Priya Patel: Any special considerations for streaming responses over PrivateLink?
08:33 Diego Alvarez: Streaming over PrivateLink works fine, but multi-chunk streaming benefits from lower jitter. Ensure long-lived TCP connections are allowed and keep-alives are enabled on the ALBs/ENIs. If you have strict idle timeouts on NAT or firewalls, that can break streams — set higher idle timeouts for streaming subnets.
08:55 Liam O'Connor: Auditability: we need request-level logs but only metadata, not PII. How do you provide that in Private?
09:02 Diego Alvarez: We provide metadata logs that include request IDs, latency buckets, model version, and usage metrics. We can ship those to your S3 via private endpoints or to a SIEM via a private connection. Full transcripts or raw outputs can be disabled by policy.
09:20 Priya Patel: Let's define a minimal deployment plan and runbook items.
09:24 Maya Chen: I'll outline a three-step plan: 1) design review (CIDR, subnets, endpoints), 2) small pilot (1 AZ, low qps), 3) scale pilot to 3 AZs and run benchmarks. Diego will run perf tests and share results.
09:39 Diego Alvarez: For the pilot, we prefer an initial setup with PrivateLink interface endpoints in one AZ, gateway endpoint for S3, ECR endpoint, and a small worker pool of two GPU instances to validate correctness. We'll instrument KV cache hits/misses and token-level latencies.
09:57 Sasha Ivanov: Regarding IAM and cross-account, how do we grant Redwood minimal privileges?
10:02 Diego Alvarez: We'll use IAM roles and an assume-role pattern with strict policies limited to EC2 ENIs, logs write to a specific S3 prefix, and KMS decrypt for specific keys if you host keys. No broad permissions. We'll provide a least-privilege template.
10:18 Priya Patel: Any considerations for multi-region DR?
10:22 Diego Alvarez: If you need regional failover, use region-local PrivateLink endpoints and replicate caches or accept a cold-warm standby in secondary region. Cross-region KV replication adds complexity and latency — we recommend a warm standby with async replication for most customers.
10:38 Maya Chen: Let's dive into a few specific Qs you raised in the run sheet — Priya asked about resolver endpoints and split-horizon. Diego, can you sketch the resolver flow?
10:47 Diego Alvarez: Flow: create Route 53 Resolver inbound endpoint in your VPC; create outbound endpoints in Redwood's VPC (if we host control plane) or vice versa if you host; then add resolver rules for your internal zones pointing to the on-prem resolver IPs. For cross-account, ensure security groups allow UDP/TCP 53 and attach resolver endpoints to specific subnets. We'll include config snippets in the runbook link.
11:12 Liam O'Connor: Do we need to open anything on our firewall for health checks?
11:15 Diego Alvarez: Health checks can be run over PrivateLink; we'll only ask to allow traffic from the ENI IPs. If you prefer, we can do pull-based checks from your side hitting our metrics endpoints — up to you.
11:26 Sasha Ivanov: One more — how do model updates work without internet?
11:30 Diego Alvarez: We can push model artifacts via S3 with gateway endpoints, or you can pull from our ECR via interface endpoint. We also support pushing artifacts into a customer S3 bucket via a secure cross-account role; that keeps artifacts in your account and avoids internet.
11:46 Priya Patel: For ECR access across accounts, do we need cross-account trust?
11:50 Diego Alvarez: You can set up an ECR replication or have our account assume a role to pull images into your account. We provide a CloudFormation stack to wire this up.
12:01 Maya Chen: Time check — still about 50 minutes left, good. Let's jump into performance detail — Diego, can you talk about token-level microbenchmarks and how network jitter shows up in p99?
12:10 Diego Alvarez: Sure. Typical token service time is compute-bound but KV lookups and network RPCs add tail latency. For example, a local cache hit might be 1-3ms, a cross-AZ cache hit 4-10ms, and a remote cross-account call 15-40ms. At high concurrency these add queuing and pile up in p95/p99. We aim to keep network RTTs minimal and recommend colocating caches and workers in same AZ when low p99s are required.
12:36 Priya Patel: For our compliance, we need KMS in our account — can Redwood use our CMKs?
12:41 Diego Alvarez: Yes. We support customer-managed keys with cross-account grants so Redwood services can decrypt artifacts without us storing keys. We'll provide the grant management steps and rotation guidance.
12:54 Liam O'Connor: Does enabling VPC Flow Logs at the level we want create cost or performance implications?
12:58 Diego Alvarez: Cost only — flow logs are write-heavy but don't affect packet forwarding. For high-volume subnets you may incur S3/CloudWatch costs. We usually recommend sampling or targeted subnets for full flow logging if cost is a concern.
13:13 Sasha Ivanov: Can you talk about fallback policies — if PrivateLink endpoint fails, what's the graceful degradation?
13:19 Diego Alvarez: We advocate multi-endpoint redundancy: multiple ENIs in different subnets/AZs. If PrivateLink to a specific AZ fails, traffic can failover to another AZ's endpoint or to Redwood Dedicated fallback (if you allow egress to a failover path). We can set health checks and automatic reroute. For strict no-internet you should allow cross-AZ PrivateLink endpoints.
13:43 Priya Patel: Will there be any changes needed to our firewall rules for ephemeral ports used by Redis-like services?
13:48 Diego Alvarez: Open the required ports for the KV store (e.g., 6379 for Redis) between the worker subnets and the KV subnets, or place KV in same security group to simplify. Use security group references rather than CIDRs to avoid brittle rules.
13:59 Maya Chen: Shane from security sometimes asks about software bill of materials and image scanning. How do you handle supply chain?
14:05 Diego Alvarez: We sign images and run image scans; we can provide SBOMs and scan reports. For Private deployments images can be pushed into your ECR after scanning in our pipeline.
14:18 Sasha Ivanov: Anything special about testing streaming under NAT timeouts?
14:22 Diego Alvarez: Lower the NAT idle timeout or pin connection pools through a proxy that maintains keep-alives. Otherwise long streaming sessions can be terminated mid-response.
14:36 Priya Patel: On the benchmarking: Diego, what should we instrument to validate p50/p90/p99?
14:41 Diego Alvarez: Token-level latency, end-to-end request latency, KV cache hit/miss ratios, batch sizes over time, GPU utilization, and queue depths. We'll provide a Grafana dashboard template.
14:54 Maya Chen: Let's walk through the pilot checklist — I'll read and you flag gaps. Step 1: Create three private subnets in 3 AZs, reserve CIDR /20 each.
15:03 Priya Patel: We may not have /20s; we probably have /22s left. Is that enough?
15:07 Diego Alvarez: /22 might be tight if you want many ENIs. For a pilot it's fine; for prod we recommend larger. We'll add guidance on expected IP consumption by worker count.
15:18 Maya Chen: Step 2: Provision interface endpoints for Redwood service and ECR in pilot AZ.
15:22 Priya Patel: We'll do that.
15:24 Maya Chen: Step 3: Create gateway endpoint for S3 and set bucket policy to allow access from the VPC endpoint. Sound ok?
15:29 Priya Patel: Yes.
15:30 Maya Chen: Step 4: Grant assume-role to Redwood for limited actions or deploy customer-managed control plane.
15:36 Sasha Ivanov: We prefer deploy-in-customer-account option.
15:38 Diego Alvarez: Great — that minimizes cross-account egress and simplifies audits. We'll send the CFN templates.
15:44 Priya Patel: Step 5: DNS resolver inbound/outbound endpoints and rules.
15:48 Diego Alvarez: We'll include the resolver template.
15:50 Liam O'Connor: On logging — we want CloudWatch metric sinks to our SIEM; can you push logs via Kinesis/firenhose?
15:57 Diego Alvarez: Yes, we can configure log delivery via Kinesis Firehose into your S3 or directly to a partner SIEM. We'll share options.
16:06 Maya Chen: Any remaining blockers?
16:09 Sasha Ivanov: We want the performance numbers in writing and a runbook for failover. Also, a security package.
16:16 Diego Alvarez: We'll produce a perf report with microbenchmarks and a runbook. Security package will include SOC2 summary, SBOM, and the KMS grant playbook.
16:27 Priya Patel: Can you show the sample CloudFormation today?
16:30 Diego Alvarez: We have a shortened sample. I'll paste the link in the chat after the call.
16:34 Sasha Ivanov: About model size — we plan to run a 13B and a 65B variant; any clear guidance on instance types?
16:40 Diego Alvarez: 13B typically runs well on a single A10x-type instance or an equivalent GPU; 65B needs multi-GPU with NVLink unless quantized aggressively. For Private we can size a dedicated pool with the required interconnect — we'll recommend instance families by model.
16:58 Priya Patel: For quantized 65B, any fallback if quality drops?
17:03 Diego Alvarez: We recommend canarying quantized variants and monitoring eval prompts. Redwood Optimize can auto-suggest when to fallback to higher-bit models based on regression alerts.
17:18 Maya Chen: Time check ~45 minutes left. Good — let's do two quick live examples: 1) DNS resolution across on-prem, 2) KV cache miss scenario across TGW. Diego, walk us through expected latencies.
17:29 Diego Alvarez: Example 1: DNS via resolver rules to on-prem adds ~10-25ms depending on VPN/Direct Connect. Example 2: KV miss across TGW to central Redis might be 20-40ms. Combined with compute you'll see p99 jumps; that's why we recommend same-AZ caches.
17:53 Liam O'Connor: If we can't colocate cache in the same AZ, what mitigations?
17:57 Diego Alvarez: Use async prefetching, larger per-worker cache windows, and lower batch sizes to keep tail latency down. Also consider an L1 in-process cache for hot entries and an L2 remote cache.
18:15 Priya Patel: For our initial pilot, can Redwood run the perf tests from within our VPC or do you need a separate test harness?
18:21 Diego Alvarez: We can deploy a small test harness into your VPC (with your permission) that simulates traffic and reports metrics. That gives the most realistic numbers.
18:31 Sasha Ivanov: Any final security concerns before we wrap?
18:34 Liam O'Connor: Just confirm that secrets don't leave our account and that audit logs are forwarded.
18:39 Diego Alvarez: Confirmed — secrets stay in your KMS, and we only request the minimal decrypt grants. Audit logs are pushed to your S3. We'll provide sample policies.
18:51 Maya Chen: Great. Quick recap and next steps: Diego will run benchmarks and share templates, Priya will send CIDRs, Liam will confirm KMS requirements, and Maya will send pricing & runbook.
19:03 Sasha Ivanov: Sounds good. Thanks all.
19:07 Diego Alvarez: I'll share the CFN link and the perf spreadsheet.
19:11 Maya Chen: I'll follow up with the security package and our pilot checklist.
19:15 Priya Patel: Thanks everyone.
19:18 End of recording. (approx 62 minutes)
